candidates.headline: A 90% SLO-attainment threshold conflicts with controlling how badly the remaining requests miss under FCFS
candidates.claim: The objective counts requests as binary pass or fail and optimizes the highest rate at which at least 90% pass. It is insensitive to the severity of failures among the other 10%. The system runs plain FCFS, which the authors acknowledge can produce a convoy effect, so some request classes can have very poor latency while goodput is reported as high.
candidates.paper_fact: In DistServe, the FCFS policy can lead to a “convoy effect”, where longer requests block shorter ones in the prefill stage.
candidates.premise: A threshold on the proportion of requests meeting an SLO constrains only how many requests violate, not by how much. Under FCFS with heterogeneous request lengths, the requests that wait behind a long job are a systematic subset and not a random one.
candidates.inference: The 10% of violating requests can be concentrated in a particular class, such as short requests stuck behind long prefills, and can miss the SLO by large margins without lowering the measured goodput. The reported per-GPU goodput therefore does not bound tail or per-class user-visible quality.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: if 9% of requests are long jobs, 90% attainment is met even when every short request queued behind a long one violates TTFT by 10x, as long as no more than 10% of requests violate.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If tail violations are severe or concentrated in one request class, an operator relying on the 90%-attainment goodput number would overestimate service quality for that class.
candidates.critical_link: A fraction-of-requests threshold is treated as adequate while the scheduler is FCFS and the paper reports no violation-severity or per-class metric.
necessary_conditions: Request lengths are heterogeneous enough to cause convoy blocking
The violating 10% is not randomly spread
The deployment cares about tail severity
defeaters: Near-uniform request lengths
Low load, where queueing is negligible
Adding preemptive scheduling, which the authors say is feasible but left out
do_not_infer: Do not infer that DistServe's tails are worse than the baselines'
Do not infer that the authors hide tail latency, since the convoy effect is disclosed
Do not infer any measured tail magnitude

candidates.headline: A weights-only memory fit check does not guarantee the decode batch size the simulator assumes
candidates.claim: Algorithm 1 admits a parallel config when the sharded weights fit in GPU memory. The paper says decode batch size is bounded by KV-cache memory. A config that passes the weights check can leave little KV room, so a decode goodput estimate that assumes a large batch could be optimistic. The excerpts do not show whether simu_decode enforces a KV-capacity limit.
candidates.paper_fact: Post-disaggregation, the batch size for decoding may be constrained by GPU memory capacity, as it is necessary to maintain the KV caches for all active requests.
candidates.premise: Decode throughput per GPU rises with batch size because decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound. Available KV space equals GPU memory minus weights and activations, so it shrinks as the per-GPU weight share grows.
candidates.inference: If simu_decode does not cap the batch by KV space, small-GPU-count configs that barely fit the weights can look best on goodput per GPU, because the per-GPU denominator is small. Such configs would have a small real batch and lower real goodput.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the simulator ignores the KV bound, the decode config chosen by Algorithm 1 would be biased toward fewer GPUs per instance. Real decode goodput would fall short of the estimate and the n:m ratio would be under-provisioned for decode.
candidates.critical_link: The feasibility predicate in Algorithm 1 (inter_op×intra_op < C) counts weights only, while the paper states that KV memory bounds the decode batch.
necessary_conditions: simu_decode does not itself enforce KV-cache capacity.
The decode batch is memory-limited rather than latency-limited at the tested workloads.
defeaters: The simulator or the latency model implicitly limits the batch by KV memory.
TPOT SLOs cap the batch before memory does.
GQA or PagedAttention reduce KV pressure enough that weights dominate.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the simulator is inaccurate. Table 2 shows less than 2% error for the configs tested, though not for Algorithm 1.
Do not infer that the chosen placements in Appendix B are infeasible. They ran on real hardware.

candidates.headline: A prefill-derived saturation length Lm does not imply a valid decode batch-size cap
candidates.claim: The paper reuses Lm, a prefill token threshold, as the largest decode batch size without giving a derivation. The decode batch limit may instead be set by KV-cache memory or the TPOT SLO.
candidates.paper_fact: For decoding instances, we set Lm as the largest batch size.
candidates.premise: Lm is a number of tokens in one forward pass, set by where prefill becomes compute-bound. A decode batch size counts requests, each adding one token per step plus a growing KV cache. Decode limits come from memory capacity, bandwidth and latency targets.
candidates.inference: The paper separately says decode batch size 'may be constrained by GPU memory capacity'. The Lm cap is therefore either not binding, when memory or TPOT limits bind first, or is an arbitrary ceiling, when they permit larger batches. The text does not say which case holds.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative, not a measurement: if KV memory only allows 200 concurrent requests and Lm = 512, the cap never binds. If memory allows 1000 requests, the cap truncates the batch at 512.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If KV-memory or TPOT-limited batch sizes fall below Lm, the decode rule has no effect. If they exceed Lm, the rule may leave decode utilization on the table.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the decode batch size allowed by KV memory and the TPOT SLO is below or above Lm for the deployed model and parallelism plan.
necessary_conditions: Decode instances run with a configuration where memory or TPOT permits a batch size different from Lm.
Lm is applied as a hard cap on decode batch size.
defeaters: Decode throughput saturates near the same value as prefill for these models, so Lm is a reasonable cap.
Memory and TPOT limits always bind first in the evaluated settings, so the cap is inert but harmless.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the cap hurts measured goodput; the paper reports no ablation of it.
Do not infer that the authors intended Lm as a memory bound.
Do not infer a specific decode limit for any model.

candidates.headline: Quadratic prefill growth does not guarantee that KV-transfer overhead shrinks in the long-context regimes the paper cites
candidates.claim: The paper argues that for long contexts the relative cost of KV transfer decreases because prefill grows quadratically. Its own appendix model, however, has a linear GEMM term and a quadratic attention term. The transfer-to-prefill ratio falls only once the quadratic term dominates, and this was not measured.
candidates.paper_fact: In such scenarios, the transmission overhead will increase as the size of the KV cache grows linearly with the prompt length. However, the prefill computation grows quadratically, so the relative duration of transmission and prefill job decreases.
candidates.premise: A sum of a linear term and a quadratic term behaves approximately linearly until the quadratic part takes over. KV bytes also grow linearly with context. In that intermediate range the transfer-to-prefill ratio is roughly flat, not falling.
candidates.inference: The appendix model for GEMM latency is proportional to the token count t, and the attention term is proportional to t squared with a small coefficient. Which term dominates depends on hidden size, block size b, and fitted constants C1 and C2. The paper does not report where the crossover lies, and evaluation used at most 2048 tokens due to OPT's positional embedding limit.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: if prefill time were 100 units of linear cost plus 0.001 times t squared, then at t=1,000 the quadratic term is 1 unit and the transfer share is unchanged from t=500. The share starts to fall only when t is on the order of 100,000.
candidates.conditional_consequence: For 10K to 100K contexts with MHA models, transfer could stay a roughly constant fraction of prefill, and in absolute terms could become large. The paper's 'remains promising' conclusion for long context would then rest on an unmeasured crossover.
candidates.critical_link: The sign of the change in the transfer-to-prefill ratio depends on the unreported crossover point between linear and quadratic prefill cost.
necessary_conditions: MHA-style KV size per token, not GQA or MQA.
Context lengths in the range where the linear GEMM term still dominates prefill.
Transfer not hidden by overlap or by NVLINK bandwidth headroom.
defeaters: Attention cost reaches dominance at moderate context lengths for the model sizes of interest.
GQA or MQA reduces KV volume by a large factor.
NVLINK bandwidth (600GB/s) is high enough to make even large transfers small relative to prefill.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that disaggregation is bad for long context.
Do not infer a specific crossover length.
Do not infer that the paper's measured ShareGPT result is affected.

candidates.headline: Per-instance goodput replication arithmetic does not guarantee balanced replica load under simple dispatch
candidates.claim: The placement algorithms size replica counts n and m by dividing traffic rate by a single-instance goodput. This presumes the dispatcher spreads requests evenly. The paper itself states equal dispatch as an assumption in its queueing discussion, but shortest-queue / least-loaded dispatch is not shown to deliver it, and scaling beyond 4 nodes is not tested.
candidates.paper_fact: substituting R with R/N assuming requests are equally dispatched to N replicas
candidates.premise: Capacity-planning by n = ceil(R / goodput) is valid only if each replica sees about R/n of the load. Dispatch imbalance makes some replicas exceed their goodput while others sit idle, and a central controller's decisions per second grow with replica count.
candidates.inference: If dispatch is imbalanced (for example, from the queue-count proxy or an undefined decode 'load'), provisioned replica counts can undershoot the SLO attainment target the simulator predicted for one instance. Agreement of simulator and real system in Table 2 does not by itself test this, because the algorithm simulates a single-instance configuration. The paper does not say whether Table 2 runs used multiple replicas or the same dispatch code.
candidates.toy_example: NOT A MEASUREMENT: two prefill replicas each sustain 4 rps at 90% attainment, so n=2 is chosen for R=8. If dispatch sends 5 rps to one replica and 3 rps to the other, the first exceeds its goodput and overall attainment can fall below 90%.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If dispatch imbalance is non-trivial at the evaluated rates, then attainment at the planned rate would be lower than the single-instance simulation suggests. If dispatch is near-balanced, replication arithmetic holds and the plan is sound.
candidates.critical_link: The plan's validity depends on the dispatcher approximating equal split, which is assumed rather than measured.

candidates.headline: A phase-level 90% goodput target does not guarantee 90% joint TTFT-and-TPOT attainment, and the 2.1x Figure 1 figure is an idealization
candidates.claim: Algorithm 1 and the Figure 1 arithmetic combine separately measured per-phase goodputs, each at 90% attainment. A request must satisfy both SLOs, and the combined system's joint attainment and transfer or queuing effects are not measured in that arithmetic.
candidates.paper_fact: Ideally, by allocating 2 GPUs for prefill and 1 GPU for decoding, we can effectively serve the model with an overall goodput of 10 rps, or equally 3.3 rps per GPU, which is 2.1x higher than existing systems.
candidates.premise: General knowledge: if a request needs both its TTFT and its TPOT to be within SLO, joint attainment is bounded by the per-phase attainments and can be lower than each of them. Combining separately measured goodputs also ignores the interaction between the two pools.
candidates.inference: Algorithm 1 selects the prefill and decode configurations independently, using simu_prefill and simu_decode, and then replicates them. Each phase is therefore tuned to its own 90% target. The Figure 1 figure is stated as 'Ideally', and its inputs are separate per-phase curves for single GPUs. It is not a measurement of the combined 3-GPU system.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: if TTFT violations and TPOT violations were independent and each phase met exactly 90%, joint attainment would be 0.9 x 0.9 = 81%. In practice the two kinds of violation are likely correlated, so the real figure would lie somewhere between 81% and 90%.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If joint attainment falls below the target at the per-phase goodput, the replicated deployment needs more GPUs than Algorithm 1 plans. The per-GPU goodput would then fall below the figure derived from the per-phase curves.
candidates.critical_link: Whether independently tuned per-phase 90% attainment translates to 90% joint attainment for the composed system.
necessary_conditions: Algorithm 1 (high node-affinity) is the one used.
Per-phase goodput is measured at a 90% target for each phase separately.
defeaters: Algorithm 2 calls simulate over the joint prefill-decode pair, so the low node-affinity path does not rely on the per-phase composition.
The end-to-end experiments (Figures 8 and 9) measure SLO attainment for whole requests, so the headline end-to-end numbers do not depend on this composition.
The simulator matched real attainment within 2% in the setups the paper tested.

candidates.headline: A small measured KV-transfer share does not imply disaggregation stays cheap on slow interconnects
candidates.claim: The reported negligible transfer cost (<0.1% of latency) holds because the low node-affinity algorithm keeps KV transfer on intra-node NVLINK. The paper's own bandwidth arithmetic shows the 25Gbps cross-node link would be far too slow for the stated load.
candidates.paper_fact: Assuming an average arrival rate of 10 rps, we need to transfer 11.3GB data per second—or equivalently 90Gbps bandwidth to render the overhead invisible.
candidates.premise: General knowledge: network transfer cost scales with KV-cache bytes per request and with request rate, and falls back to the slowest link on the path if placement cannot confine it to a fast one.
candidates.inference: The testbed's cross-node bandwidth is 25Gbps, below the 90Gbps the paper computes for 10 rps with OPT-66B. The low measured transfer share therefore depends on Algorithm 2 keeping prefill and decode segments of the same stage on one node. If a model, GPU count per node or memory budget prevents that colocation, KV traffic would cross the slow link. Savings from removing interference would then be offset by transfer delay.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: with an effective 25Gbps link, moving a 1.13GB KV cache takes roughly 0.36s. That is already above a 0.25s TTFT-scale SLO if it lands on the critical path.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If placement cannot keep each stage's prefill and decode segments within a node, for example with fewer or smaller GPUs per node or a very large model, then the interference savings may be partly or fully offset by KV-transfer delay.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the intra-node placement constraint of Algorithm 2 can be satisfied in the deployment, so that KV transfer avoids the slow cross-node link.
necessary_conditions: The cluster has low cross-node bandwidth.
Prefill and decode segments of the same stage cannot all be placed on one node.
The KV size is large (MHA, long prompts) and the request rate is high.
defeaters: The cluster has high-speed InfiniBand, and Algorithm 1 is then used.
The model uses GQA or MQA, which shrinks the KV cache; the paper states that this lowers transmission overhead.
Pull-based transfer and asynchronous copies may hide some of the delay.

Do not infer that OPT-175B in the tested setup suffers from transfer cost.

candidates.headline: Higher per-GPU goodput at 90% attainment does not imply or guarantee proportionally lower cost per query or guaranteed SLO satisfaction
candidates.claim: The paper uses per-GPU goodput at a 90% SLO-attainment target as a direct proxy for cost per query and states 'up to 7.4× lower cost per LLM query'. That conversion holds only if the number of provisioned GPUs is the sole cost. The 90% target also does not guarantee SLO satisfaction for every request.
candidates.paper_fact: higher per-GPU goodput directly translates into lower cost per query
candidates.premise: Serving cost in general includes other components such as heterogeneous GPU prices, idle capacity, networking and CPU. A rate-ratio improvement measured per GPU becomes a cost-ratio improvement of the same size only if cost is strictly proportional to GPU count.
candidates.inference: The paper's cost claim depends on counting GPUs only. Disaggregation holds a separate copy of the weights for each phase and sizes replicas by rounding up, which can leave capacity idle. The cost-per-query ratio can therefore differ from the goodput ratio. Because 90% attainment is the target, 'guaranteed satisfaction of SLOs' can hold at most for the fraction of requests that meet the SLOs, not for all requests.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: if the required rate is 10 rps and per-replica goodput is 4 rps, ceil(10/4)=3 replicas are provisioned (12 rps of capacity). Roughly a sixth of capacity is idle, so cost per query is higher than 'GPUs times goodput' suggests.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If cost has components that do not scale with GPU count, or if replica rounding leaves capacity idle, the realized cost reduction at deployment is smaller than the reported goodput ratio.
candidates.critical_link: Cost per query is proportional to provisioned GPU count and nothing else, and a 90% attainment threshold is an adequate stand-in for service quality.

candidates.headline: Per-phase 90% SLO attainment does not imply 90% joint attainment
candidates.claim: Algorithm 1 sizes prefill and decode separately, each at the SLO attainment target in its own metric (TTFT or TPOT). Requests must meet both SLOs, so the replicated system's joint attainment can fall below the target. Adding headroom to restore it costs extra GPUs, which cuts into the per-GPU goodput the algorithm is meant to maximize.
candidates.paper_fact: to attain phase-level optimal per-gpu goodput; then, we use replication to match the overall traffic rate.
candidates.premise: If a request fails TTFT or fails TPOT, it fails the SLO. Joint attainment is therefore at least 1 minus the sum of the two per-phase violation rates (a union bound), and it equals the per-phase value only if the violations coincide perfectly.
candidates.inference: Prefill at 90% TTFT attainment and decode at 90% TPOT attainment can give joint attainment anywhere from 80% to 90%. Which end applies depends on how the two violation sets overlap. Reaching 90% jointly would need stricter per-phase targets, hence more or larger instances.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: if 10% of requests miss TTFT and a different 10% miss TPOT, joint attainment is 80%. If the same 10% miss both, it is 90%.

candidates.headline: Shortest-queue prefill dispatch does not imply shortest waiting time under variable prompt lengths

candidates.inference: Count-based shortest-queue dispatch can place a request behind a few very long prompts while an instance holding many short prompts looks busier. Prefill replicas then become unevenly loaded, raising TTFT tail and lowering SLO attainment on length-diverse workloads.

candidates.headline: Pull-based buffering in prefill GPU memory does not imply stability under sustained decode backlog
candidates.claim: Moving the KV queue from the decode side to the prefill side protects decode instances from memory overload during short bursts. The paper states no bound on the buffer and no admission or throttle rule.

candidates.headline: Monitoring average lengths and arrival rate does not guarantee detecting shifts that change the best placement
candidates.claim: The replanning trigger watches average input/output length and average arrival rate, but the placement is computed from the full fitted length and arrival distributions. candidates.premise: A mean is a lossy summary of a distribution. Queueing delay, pipeline bubbles, and SLO attainment at a percentile target depend on spread and tails, not only on means.
candidates.inference: The placement search uses a simulator fed by a fitted distribution of lengths and arrivals, and the paper says non-uniform lengths cause pipeline bubbles that deviate from the uniform-length analysis. So two workloads with equal means but different dispersion can have different best (parallelism, replica) configurations. A mean-based trigger can miss this. The trailing 'etc.' leaves open that other statistics are also monitored, but none are named.

candidates.headline: Replanning being faster than hourly drift does not guarantee it is net-beneficial under faster shifts
candidates.claim: The paper justifies replanning by comparing search and reload time with the hourly scale of workload change. It gives no shift threshold, hysteresis, or cost-benefit rule, and it does not quantify downtime against the gain from a new placement. If shifts are faster than reload-plus-search time, or the reload gain is small, replanning can chase the workload and spend more time reloading than serving.
candidates.paper_fact: This process is expedient – the proposed algorithm runs in seconds (§6.5) and reloading LLM weights can be completed within minutes – far shorter than the hourly scale at which real-world workload variations tend to occur.
candidates.premise: Net benefit of a reconfiguration is the gain in goodput over the period the new placement stays valid, minus the service disruption during weight reloading and re-provisioning. Without a stopping rule, a trigger that fires on every perturbation can pay the disruption cost repeatedly.
candidates.inference: The 'significant pattern shift' trigger has no stated threshold, and no hysteresis or in-flight request handling is described. The paper's own timing is mixed: the text says 'seconds', while §4.1 says under 1.3 minutes in the largest setting and §6.5 says the execution time is 'in minutes'. Figure 12 shows search time growing with GPU count, and reload time plausibly grows with model size. For large models, large clusters, or flash-crowd regimes, the hourly-scale justification may no longer hold.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: suppose search plus reload takes 5 minutes of degraded service and the workload oscillates every 8 minutes. Almost every window would be spent transitioning to a placement that is already stale.
candidates.conditional_consequence: Under shifts that are not slow relative to reload-plus-search time, periodic replanning could lower effective goodput below that of a static placement. The paper does not bound this regime.
candidates.critical_link: Search-plus-reload time being much smaller than the shift timescale is sufficient for replanning to be net-beneficial, and the hourly-scale assumption holds for the deployments of interest.

Reload can be overlapped with serving or done with rolling replacement (not described in the paper)
An undisclosed threshold or hysteresis exists in the implementation

candidates.premise: SLO attainment counts each request against its own deadline, whereas FCFS orders requests by arrival only, so it does not minimize the number of missed deadlines.
candidates.inference: When long and short prompts mix, a long prompt at the head can push short prompts past a TTFT deadline they could have met if served first. Reported attainment then depends on the length mix and the TTFT SLO tightness.
candidates.toy_example: NOT A MEASUREMENT: a 15 s prefill arrives just before ten 0.1 s prefills with a 1 s TTFT SLO. FCFS makes all ten miss; serving them first would meet all ten at a small cost to the long request.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If a workload mixes very long and short prompts under a TTFT SLO comparable to a long prompt's execution time, FCFS attainment will drop below what a length- or deadline-aware order could reach. If the SLO is loose relative to the longest prefill (as for LongBench's 15 s TTFT), the effect is muted.
candidates.critical_link: The convoy delay matters only when the TTFT deadline is shorter than the blocking prefill time.
necessary_conditions: Heterogeneous prompt lengths within one queue
TTFT SLO not much larger than long-prompt prefill time
Queueing occurs (non-trivial load)
defeaters: Loose TTFT SLO relative to prefill time
Homogeneous request lengths
Low load where queues are short
Preemption, which the authors say is feasible but not implemented
do_not_infer: That the authors' headline speedups over vLLM or DeepSpeed-MII are due to or invalidated by FCFS
That baselines are better at this because they use different scheduling
A magnitude for the effect
candidates.lens: L2+L6 (deadline-agnostic ordering; cost shifted to short requests)
